title: Plugin4Shell: one bug breaks SHA pinning in Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Gemini CLI
subtitle: AIR Security disclosed a zero-click RCE in the four leading AI coding agents on September 18 — Claude Code and Codex are patched, Gemini CLI is being retired without a fix, and GitHub Copilot is still exposed.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: AIR Security disclosed a zero-click remote code execution vulnerability on September 18, dubbed Plugin4Shell, affecting the four leading AI coding agents: Anthropic Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Google Gemini CLI. The bug defeats SHA pinning, the mechanism marketplaces use to lock an installed plugin to a specific reviewed commit hash. An attacker who controls a plugin's repository can create a Git branch whose name matches the 40-character commit hash the marketplace has pinned. During plugin install or update, Git's reference resolution prefers the matching ref name over the actual commit object, and the agent installs the malicious branch while its logs report a successful SHA-pinned install.

The zero-click part is the automatic-update path. Claude Code and Codex update installed plugins in the background by default, so an affected user did not need to run a command or click a link for the malicious code to land. Once the compromised plugin loads, it runs with the coding agent's ambient permissions — read the working repo, exfiltrate credentials from the shell environment, open outbound connections. AIR called this the first true supply-chain vulnerability in the AI agent ecosystem, and the description fits: it exploits a shared assumption across four independent products, not a bug in any one of them.

The patch situation is uneven. Anthropic shipped a fix in Claude Code 2.1.179, OpenAI shipped one in Codex 0.146.0, both released on September 18. Google said it will not fix Gemini CLI because it has already deprecated the product and recommends users migrate to Antigravity — a defensible choice, but one that leaves current Gemini CLI users exposed with no upgrade path inside the same tool. GitHub has not yet released a Copilot fix as of Sunday, and its plugin marketplace is the largest of the four by installed base. Anyone running Copilot's plugin ecosystem in production should assume compromise is possible until a patch lands.

Takeaway for learners — the interesting lesson is not the specific bug, it is where the industry's implicit trust model just broke. Every AI coding agent shipped with 'we pin plugins to a reviewed commit' as a security backstop, and every one of them made the same assumption about how Git resolves references. That's what a shared-assumption bug looks like, and it is a preview of the next several years: coding agents install more code, run it faster, and touch more of your environment than any previous developer tool. Turn off automatic plugin updates where you can. Review your agent's plugin permissions the same way you review a browser extension's — not the same way you review a package on npm.
